=== README
# claudinite-fleet-sheepdog

The fleet **enforcer** marker — declaring it makes a repo the one that covers and maintains every repo
under an owner. Opt-in (a dedicated claudinite-fleet-sheepdog repo declares it; **not** seeded by `--init`). It
standardizes the fleet coverage that used to be bespoke Claudinite infrastructure into a declaration.

Thin by design: prose + the config schema (the claudinite-fleet-sheepdog pack entry's `config` = `{ owner, kind, exclude,
canonRepo, packSeeds }`) + five cross-repo **sweeps/levers**, each a
scheduled task whose sweep is its `code_work`. The pack carries **no workflow**, and nothing agentic
happens *here* — it happens in the *member*, on the fan-out model
([#749](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/749)) — the enforcer dispatches, the
member executes:

| sweep | task | asks |
|---|---|---|
| [check-fleet-roster.mjs](tasks/fleet-roster/check-fleet-roster.mjs) → [adoption-issues.mjs](tasks/fleet-roster/adoption-issues.mjs) + [freshness.mjs](tasks/fleet-roster/freshness.mjs) | [fleet-roster](tasks/fleet-roster/README.md) (daily) | is this repo a **member**, and is that membership still **meaning** anything? → adoption issues + the run report's freshness section |
| [scan-for-needed-packs.mjs](tasks/fleet-add-missing-packs/scan-for-needed-packs.mjs) + [force-add-packs.mjs](tasks/fleet-add-missing-packs/force-add-packs.mjs) | [fleet-add-missing-packs](tasks/fleet-add-missing-packs/README.md) (weekly, and forceable) | which packs is a member missing — the ones its **shape** suspects, or the ones the owner named? → a work-list issue *in* each member + that member's scheduler fired; the member's own agent adopts |
| [check-fleet-pack-seeds.mjs](tasks/fleet-pack-seeds/check-fleet-pack-seeds.mjs) | [fleet-pack-seeds](tasks/fleet-pack-seeds/README.md) (daily) | does a member declare what this fleet **standardizes on**? → the declaration, written |
| [force-fleet-baseline.mjs](tasks/fleet-baseline/force-fleet-baseline.mjs) | [fleet-baseline](tasks/fleet-baseline/README.md) (`manual` — forced runs only) | make every member baseline **now**, then follow each to canon's published versions → an outcome table, not a dispatch count |

**The roster carries two questions** because they are asked of the same repos from the same walk
([#788](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/788)). The freshness half exists because
per-project scheduling made every member maintain itself and, in doing so, removed the last thing that
looked at a member from the **outside** — self-maintenance cannot detect its own absence. It used to be
its own weekly task with its own enumeration, and re-derived the coverage it claimed to take as given;
the two then classified the same repo differently (an excluded repo carrying a declaration read
*covered* to one and *out of scope* to the other), and each half's `unknown` failed its own run knowing
nothing of the other's. What is still split is the two **issue families** — they close on unrelated
conditions — not the walk.

**Missing-packs** exists because a pack's `detect` fingerprint is consulted **once**, at
bootstrap's `--init`: baselining backfills the seeded packs and each declared pack's `requires`
closure, but never re-fingerprints, so a member that grows into a pack after adoption is never told
the pack exists and the owner has to already know what to ask for. **Pack-seeds** is the only one that **writes** to a
member: some packs need a parameter no member can derive, because the answer is a fact about the
*fleet* — and canon cannot supply it either, since a bootstrap run does not know which fleet it is
bootstrapping into. This repo's `packSeeds` config lists what its members should declare, and the
sweep converges that list. It names no pack itself: the fleet supplies every id.

**The pack-seed sweep stays narrow on purpose**: one declaration from `packSeeds`, one PUT to the
member's default branch guarded by the blob sha the read returned, idempotent, no issue in either
direction. Three properties keep it safe. It **names no pack** — every id comes from config, so the
enforcer never becomes a second place packs are known. It **gates on the member's own mount**: a
declared pack whose code is absent is a blocking `config` error there, and a member's mount carries
only what it declared as of its last converge, so the sweep writes only where the pack is already on
disk — `not-vendored` is a wait rather than a finding, and members converge nightly, so a rollout
needs no coordination. And it **seeds, never overrides**: a member that already declares the pack, or
already carries a config for it, keeps both. The fleet's list is a floor, and a choice a repo made is
a decision the sweep cannot second-guess.

That is also why the enforcer states a seeded pack's config **twice** — in `packSeeds`, and in its
own entry for that pack — and why `seeds-agree` holds the two to each other. Nothing compares them at
seed time, and a member has no way to know what the enforcer kept for itself, so an enforcer running
one configuration while the fleet runs another is silent until someone looks.

A pack arriving *with* canon reaches the fleet that already exists through a **baseline migration**
instead — a `declarePacks` op applied by each member's own update run, in the same transactional
commit that vendors the pack's code. The sweep is the **standing** half: a migration record is dated
and retires, while the sweep keeps converging every member the fleet acquires after it is gone.

The fit sweep fingerprints against a scratch clone of `canonRepo`, never against this repo's own
mount — the mount carries only the packs the enforcer declares, and sweeping against it would report
every member as fitted while testing almost nothing. Its report names the corpus it measured against,
so a shrunken denominator is visible rather than silent.

**The fit sweep's agent stage splits the way every one here does** — everything decidable in code
stays in the agentless `code_work`, and the agent is reached only for the part that is genuinely a
judgment. Here it is a judgment plus a repo edit — confirming the
suspicion and running the [adopt-pack](../claudinite-lifecycle/skills/adopt-pack/SKILL.md) skill against the member —
while enumerate, fingerprint and converge-the-issues stay in code. That one opens the PR and lands it
unattended there (#1453): declaring a pack switches on conformance checks that run in that member's
CI from the moment they land, and gate the merge.

**No agent anywhere here reaches another repo**, and that is the trust model rather than an
implementation detail ([#749](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/749)). The first
missing-packs design ended in an enforcer-side agent stage, and its very first production run parked because the enforcer's executor is — correctly — scoped to the enforcer repo alone.
What crosses a repo boundary is an issue and a `workflow_dispatch`, both over `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`;
the deprecated task-level `session_scope` ([the writing-tasks skill](../claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md)) has no
place here.

A member whose **scheduler is dormant** (`dormant` on its own `claudinite-tasks` pack entry) is out of
**every upkeep question this pack asks** (owner, 2026-09-13): out of the fit sweep, out of the usage
denominator, never written to by the pack-seed sweep, not measured by the roster's freshness half, and
dispatched by no fleet-wide operation. Its silence says nothing about any skill; recommending it a pack
would be recommending work it has declared it is not doing; a commit landed in it from outside is the
upkeep it opted out of; and a mount nothing will ever converge cannot be behind in a way anyone is
going to fix — a freshness verdict on one is a finding with no owner. It stays a **member**: membership
is unchanged, because dormancy is about upkeep, not membership, and the coverage census names it under
`dormant`. The one lever that still reaches one is the hand-typed `INCLUDE_DORMANT=true` on a
[fleet-baseline](tasks/fleet-baseline/README.md) item — a person asking for it by name.

A repo the fleet was told to **ignore** (`config.exclude`) is out further still: no sweep reads it at
all, so none of them learns whether it even carries a declaration, and every report names it once under
`ignored` and claims nothing else about it. A force that names one is refused rather than written
around — the remedy is to take the repo off the list.

**Every report enumerates the full fleet.** Whatever a repo's state — covered, dormant, uncovered,
excluded, archived, a fork, inactive today, or simply not measured by that sweep — each sweep's
report names it under exactly one state rather than dropping it. A roster that names only the
exceptions has silent holes, and a reader cannot tell "fine" from "fell out of the report": the
roster's coverage section lists covered members (dormant ones flagged) alongside the uncovered, and its
freshness section names its fresh members and its out-of-scope repos with why; the fit sweep names the members that came
back **fitted** as loudly as the ones with findings, and names the fingerprints it could not decide
from outside rather than counting them as non-matches; the usage sweep's `coverage` section
accounts for every repo under the owner and its run report flags folding members with no captured
activity that day; fleet-baseline reports every repo it did *not* dispatch, with the reason, and every repo it DID dispatch that never reached canon's versions.

**Undecidable is not a non-match.** Most fingerprints are answerable from a path listing, and the fit
sweep answers those over one tree call per member; one that reads file *contents* is resolved by a
bounded prefetch of exactly the files it asked for, and one that greps every source file exceeds that
budget and is reported **undecided**. The member's own agent — which has the repo checked out —
settles those exactly ([fingerprint-fit.mjs](tasks/fleet-add-missing-packs/fingerprint-fit.mjs)). A
truncated tree listing makes every non-match on that repo undecided for the same reason: "we did not
look" and "we looked and it isn't there" are different facts, and only one is safe to act on.

**A sweep that cannot see a repo says so and fails.** A repo whose declaration the roster cannot read
is `unknown` to both its questions, never uncovered and never behind; a member whose mount probe
fails is `unknown` to freshness alone, because its declaration was read and the coverage verdict
stands; a member the fit scan cannot read is `unknown`, never fitted; a member whose scheduler
refused a fan-out dispatch is named and fails the run, because a work list nobody will act on is not
a green outcome; and a member the pack-seed sweep cannot reach opens no issue, closes none on its
behalf, and exits non-zero. A non-zero preprocessing subprocess fails the task, and the scheduler
parks one open issue for it.

**The two operator levers ride the work-item queue, not a workflow.** `fleet-baseline` is the first
task declaring `trigger: request`: not on the schedule, never asked at any tick, it runs only from
an item the owner creates by hand — `create-work-item claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/fleet-baseline`, with `REPOS=…`, `DRY_RUN=true`,
`INCLUDE_DORMANT=true`, `FOLLOW_MINUTES=…` as `--context` lines — which wakes every covered member's own
standing `update` item so the fleet picks canon up now instead of over the next day. A forced
fleet-add-missing-packs item is the second lever, same command, its own Context.

**`fleet-baseline` reports outcomes, not dispatches**
([#1293](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1293)). A dispatch POST returning 204 says a
run was queued and nothing more, and a report built from those 204s describes the sweep's own outgoing
calls while reading as fleet-wide delivery — a run announced `13 fired, 0 failed` where 9 of the 13 took
nothing ([#1292](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1292)). So after firing, the sweep
follows each member until its own declaration stamps the engine and every declared pack at the versions
canon publishes, and reports each as `converged`, `already-current`, `did-not-converge`, `never-started`
or `unknown`. A member already at canon's versions is a success in its own right: its update correctly
declines, and it does no work. *Current* is a claim about **published version numbers** — canon content
that shipped without a version bump moves no number and is invisible to it, which the report says itself.

This is not the 2026-08-11 follow returning. That one was a blind fixed wait every run paid whatever the
fleet was doing, and it forced the lever to be a standalone workflow with a `.github/` managed copy
([#749](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/749),
[`2026-08-11-fleet-baseline-task`](migrations/2026-08-11-fleet-baseline-task/migration.mjs)).
[follow-to-current.mjs](tasks/fleet-baseline/follow-to-current.mjs) polls a real terminal condition
instead: each member leaves the loop the moment it reads current, so an already-current fleet finishes
on the first pass in seconds, and the lever stays an ordinary queue task.

Each sweep lives **inside its task's folder**, because nothing outside that task uses it. Only what
they all share sits at the pack root: [fleet-api.mjs](fleet-api.mjs) (the cross-repo REST
primitives, including the one that fires a member's scheduler),
[fleet-config.mjs](fleet-config.mjs) (the one reader of this pack's entry `config`) and
[fleet-token.mjs](fleet-token.mjs) (the one statement of what `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` must be granted —
every "token is not set" message, the adoption handover step and a `403`'s hint are rendered from its
table, so no sweep ever states a subset of its own).

The rest of the machinery — running the daily-run, the task engine (`packs/claudinite-tasks/`), scheduling —
is Claudinite **core**. What a session in an enforcer repo has to get right: [RULES.md](RULES.md).

## Config

The enforcer's `.claudinite-settings.json` carries, as its `packs` entry for this pack:

```json
{ "id": "claudinite-fleet-sheepdog", "config": { "owner": "missingbulb", "kind": "user", "exclude": ["owner/repo-a"],
                                "canonRepo": "missingbulb/Claudinite",
                                "packSeeds": [{ "id": "<a pack>", "config": { … } }] } }
```

| key | default | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| `owner` | this repo's owner | whose repositories make up the fleet |
| `kind` | `"user"` | org support is a later addition |
| `exclude` | none | the repos deliberately kept out, a full `owner/name` each |
| `canonRepo` | `<owner>/Claudinite` | what a member's installed versions are measured against — named rather than inferred, because a version tells you nothing about where it came from |
| `packSeeds` | none | what this fleet wants every member to declare, each `{ id, config? }`. The **only** place a pack is named: the sweep carries the mechanism, the fleet carries the choice |

Every key defaults, so an existing claudinite-fleet-sheepdog config keeps working untouched.
[fleet-config.mjs](fleet-config.mjs) is the one reader of all of it.

## How the tasks are wired

Ordinary **pack tasks**, not fleet mechanisms. Their *implementation* — an account-spanning PAT —
happens to scan every repo under the owner, but their declaration, scheduling and lifecycle are
exactly those of any pack task. None declares the `fleet` signal: the cross-repo reach lives in the
implementation, never in how a task is wired.

| task | when it runs | agent | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fleet-roster` | `due:daily` | none | none |
| `fleet-add-missing-packs` | `due:weekly` (forceable) | none | none |
| `fleet-pack-seeds` | `due:daily` | none | none |
| `fleet-baseline` | never — no `preconditions`; only from an item the owner creates | none | none |

The cadences follow what each question can change on. Roster is daily on its coverage question, and
its freshness half rides along rather than gating on a weekly clock it would have to compute; pack
seeds is daily because a member becomes writable the moment its nightly converge vendors the pack,
which makes daily mean "the next morning".

Every ceiling here is `none`. The pack-seed sweep's write goes to **other** repos, and the ceiling
describes what a task may do to its own. What only a repo edit can finish is the member's own
adopt-requested-packs task's, which opens the PR and lands it unattended *there* (#1453).

There is **no coverage workflow**: preprocessing runs Action-side inside the repo's one scheduler
workflow, where the Actions secret is already reachable, and each task's
`code_work_required_secrets: ['FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN']` stamps the name into that workflow's env — which is what
asks the owner for it. A workflow that exists only to hold a secret is redundant
([the writing-tasks skill](../claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md)).

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Acting on an add-packs work-list issue | high | correctness | prose: <100 words |
| Acting on a scanned pack suggestion | medium | correctness | prose: <100 words |
| Reading unknown in a report | high | correctness | prose: <100 words |
| Judging whether a member is behind | high | correctness | prose: <100 words |
| Answering why the fleet did not move | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words |
| Pushing canon to the whole fleet now | low | complexity | prose: <200 words |
| Adding a pack across the fleet | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words |
| Granting or repairing FLEETGITHUBTOKEN | high | correctness | prose: <100 words |
| A sweep reporting 403 or no-permission | medium | complexity | prose: <50 words |

The config rules (`exclude`, `packSeeds`, the declaration a seed must agree with) are the
[`configuring-the-fleet`](skills/configuring-the-fleet/SKILL.md) skill, forced for
`.claudinite-settings.json`.

## Skills

| Skill | Trigger |
|---|---|
| [`configuring-the-fleet`](skills/configuring-the-fleet/SKILL.md) | any edit of `.claudinite-settings.json` in the fleet-enforcer repo — held by the guard until loaded |

## Checks

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fleet-pack-seed-agrees` | medium | correctness | check: blocking |

---
name: writing-wiki-pages
description: How a product-wiki page is written and grown — the Key insights header, citation, what a source actually supports (attribution, independent voices, public proxies), correction without deletion, the growth log, sample-data, when a pass writes nothing. Loaded for any edit under product-wiki/.
metadata:
  body: guidelines
  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
    - "product-wiki/**"
---

# Writing product-wiki pages

The rules a wiki page is held to while it is being edited. Which page to grow and where the
material comes from is the caller's business — the weekly
[wiki-growth](../../tasks/wiki-growth/task.md) pass picks from each page's open questions, and
[explore-link](../explore-link/SKILL.md) is handed a source — and both write under these.

- **Opening a page with what it found.** `## Key insights` leads the page: a few bullets carrying
  the research's actual conclusions — the numbers, the competitor that already does this, the
  thing that turned out not to be true — enough that a human who reads only the header
  understands what was researched and what it means. Not a table of contents ("covers pricing
  and competitors"), not a teaser. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and
  citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to. (opening-page-found)

- **Writing an insight bullet.** One short line, in ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no
  citation, no hedge, no jargon a newcomer would have to decode. Prefer the finding that would
  *surprise* someone who knows the field: the thing that turned out not to be true, the number
  nobody expects, the competitor who already shipped it. Whether a point is obvious is genuinely
  hard to call, so **don't agonise — when in doubt, keep it**. A borderline-obvious line costs
  the reader two seconds; a long, careful line costs them the header. (writing-insight-bullet)

- **Touching the header after a pass.** It is a current view, not a log. A pass that changes
  what a page's most important findings are rewrites the header to match — a superseded insight
  leaves it (the correction and its why stay in the body, per below), and an insight the pass
  didn't touch stays put. If nothing changed the page's top-line understanding, the header
  doesn't move. (touching-header-pass)

- **Starting a pass on a page.** Compile once, refine in place: read the target page end to end
  before researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as open, thin,
  or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass. Never re-derive a claim that's
  already cited and current. (starting-pass-page)

- **Writing a claim.** Cited, never silently rewritten: an uncited claim doesn't get written. A
  wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source), never deleted
  without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's growth log and updates the open
  questions in both directions. (writing-claim)

- **Attributing a figure you saw in several places.** Recurrence is not evidence of who
  published it: search snippets quote each other, so a number that recurs across five results
  is one source repeated, and the firm the snippets name is routinely not the firm that produced
  it. When you cannot open the report, attribute the figure to the publisher a source
  explicitly names as its **origin**; when sources disagree about that, say so on the page
  rather than picking one. (attributing-figure-saw)

- **Quoting a person.** Attribute it to the speaker, and read an asker's or author's framing as
  theirs alone: a leading question carries the interviewer's hypothesis, a case study carries the
  vendor's, and the quote answering one is evidence only of what the respondent chose to say
  inside it. Where the source won't let you tell who introduced a term, say so beside the
  quote. (quoting-person)

- **Counting how many people back a finding.** Count independent voices, not mentions: one
  thread's ten replies, or a case study and the vendor's post about it, are one voice, and a
  theme one named customer raised says that rather than "users report". A count you cannot
  establish is absent, not "several". (counting-many-people)

- **Researching what this product's own users need.** Review sites, forum threads and
  competitors' testimonials are evidence about *other people's* customers, and a page built only
  from them satisfies every check while reading as a finding about yours — so name the proxy in
  the claim, and leave the question it cannot answer standing in `## Open questions` rather than
  letting the page imply it is answered. (researching-products-users)

- **Finding nothing citable.** No fabricated growth: most passes find little or nothing; no new
  citable material → no edit, no log entry, no PR. (finding-nothing-citable)

- **Adding to `product-wiki/sample-data/`, or a new wiki folder.** sample-data gains a file only
  when a wiki claim needs one to point to — never test fixtures (anything a test asserts against
  belongs in engineering's tree). Any folder under `product-wiki/` outside the two reserved
  names *is* a wiki (the structural classifier), so create one only deliberately, seeded with
  its required sections; automation refines existing pages, it never invents new ones.
  (adding-product-wiki)

- **Touching `product-wiki/product-requirements/`.** The sink is human-reviewed only, and it
  never changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding that
  should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and waits for a human.
  (touching-product-wiki)

- **Landing the change.** Unattended growth always lands as an unmerged PR — researched claims
  entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate. The owner phrase **"grow the
  product wiki"** runs the worker method in-session with full web tooling: same rules, same PR
  discipline. (landing-change)

{"number":1060,"title":"Collapse chrome-extension-release into chrome-extension, and stop packs discussing each other","body":"Closes #1057. Four commits: the engine tolerance, the collapse, the reference sweep, and the cross-pack prose purge.

## The design question the issue named

Merging an opt-in release standard into an always-on coding pack looks like it turns the release checks on for every extension repo. It does not, because **the release half's activation was always structural** — `chrome-extension-release`'s `detect` was the orchestrator workflow's name, and declaring the pack was a second copy of that same fact which each repo had to remember to write.

So the fact is now read where it is used: `shipsReleasePipeline` gates the coded rule, all seven `cer/` declared checks carry the same test as their `relevantWhen`, and `store-release`'s precondition asks it of the `release` signal. A repo that only *codes* an extension is asked for no release config, no privacy page and no README release sections. A repo that publishes gets all of it without declaring anything.

**Two signals, either one enough** — the orchestrator's `name:`, or a `.github/release.config`. Each alone leaves the rule that judges it unreachable: gate only on the name and a repo that renamed its orchestrator loses every release check *including the one that tells it to rename it back*; gate only on the config and `cer/release-config`, whose whole job is a missing config, can never fire. The orchestrator is matched by name and never by path, because the canon hosts files at those paths and would otherwise fingerprint itself.

The gate is spelled three times — the coded rule, the JSON (which cannot import), and the scheduler signal (the engine may not import a pack) — so a test runs all three over one matrix of repo shapes and fails if any copy drifts. Seen failing on each copy in turn.

## Members

`RENAMED_PACKS` gains `chrome-extension-release → chrome-extension`, so a member activates the right pack the moment the mount lands, declaration converged or not; a pack-owned record at `chrome-extension` version 3 converges the declaration itself. No engine version bump, so no canary release gate is involved.

The rename **collides on every member**, because the absorbed pack's `requires` meant everyone declaring it declared the survivor too. `applyPackRenames` now merges instead of producing a duplicate: first occurrence keeps its position, its own values win a conflict, arrays union, and an object absorbed into a plain-string entry promotes it. Dropping either side would drop the member's own `config`, `rules` and `accept` — acceptances especially, since a dropped one brings its finding straight back.

**The `cer/` ids do not change**, for the same reason: `accept` entries name rules by id.

## A pack does not discuss its neighbours

Reviewing the collapse turned up the wider class: `firebase-release`'s README opened by saying it is declared "like chrome-extension". A `barriers` probe (`siblings: "packs"` → `packs/*`) found **51 such crossings across 22 packs**, in two shapes:

- **Boundary/turf prose** — "sits under X", "that is Y's turf", a whole `## Boundary` section listing what the neighbours own. Purged. It is a second copy of what `ruleRoutingGuidance.excludes` already carries in one machine-read field — the field the pack directory routes a lesson by — so each site now states what the pack does *not* cover without naming who does.
- **Procedure pointers** — a rule delegating a how-to to another pack's skill, a check's `doc:` field, an executable command, and the comments on the dashboard's deliberate duplicates of sheepdog's helpers. Kept: the link is what makes the procedure findable, and restating it in both places is exactly what the corpus forbids.

22 references survive, all in the second class. No standing barrier rule was added — the probe was a measuring instrument, and it is not in the diff.

## Consumer safety

The shape the collapse newly exposes is an extension repo that codes but does not publish — the canon publishes no extension, so its own CI says nothing about it. `packs-tests/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs` gains that shape (`codes-an-extension`), and a pack test asserts every release rule is inert on it.

## Folders touched

- **`engine/pack_loader/`, `engine/migrations/`** — the rename-map entry and the merge in `applyPackRenames`.
- **`engine/scheduler/signals/`** — the `release` signal carries whether the repo publishes, read off the checkout beside the manifest version it already read.
- **`packs/chrome-extension/`** — absorbs the release module, the seven declared checks (each gated), the stubs, the `store-release` task, both migration records, and `RELEASE.md` as the **`chrome-store-releases`** skill; manifest, README and RULES rewritten for one pack.
- **`packs/firebase`, `firebase-release`, `google-identity`, `jwt`, `web-speech`, `headless-browser`, `executable-requirements`, `spec-driven-product`, `web-scraping`, `git-github`, `sheepdog`, `claudinite-growth`, `claudinite-lifecycle`, `basics`** — neighbour prose removed, and in the release packs' case references to the pack that no longer exists.
- **`.github/`** — the core workflows README, and the retired pre-vendoring release copies' own naming.
- **`packs-tests/rehearsal/`** — the fixture shape above.
- Versions bumped on every pack whose content changed; `packs/directory.GENERATED.md` re-rendered by its test.

The two migration records keep their wording — they describe arrangements true when they were written.

## Verification

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2200 pass, 0 fail.
- `check_the_work --changed --base origin/main` — exit 0.
- `check_the_world` — 0 blocking, 61 advisory (all pre-existing).
- The merge and both drift-guard directions seen red before the code that fixes them; the crossing count re-measured after the purge.

=== README ===
# flutter pack

Active when the repo has `pubspec.yaml`. Durable, project-agnostic Flutter practices in
`RULES.md`, earned in missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers: ports-and-adapters out of the widget tree
(with the committed import-boundary test and the shipped fake world), widget-test/golden mechanics
(real fonts, no `pumpAndSettle` on spinners, injectable fetchers, fixed viewport, the async-epoch
guard), and toolchain habits (pub-cache API verification, zero-issue analyze, stall-robust test
runners for sandboxes). Prose, two checks and two skills — the enforceable pieces the pack cannot
judge from outside (import scan, coverage gates) live as committed tests inside the consuming
project.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Widgets depend on ports, never on plugins. | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words |
| Enforce the boundary with an import scan | medium | complexity | prose: <50 words |
| Ship the fakes in the package | low | complexity | prose: <100 words |
| Extract the root shell into a widget | low | complexity | prose: <50 words |
| Anything that fetches must be injectable | medium | complexity | prose: <50 words + check (`flutter/network-fetch-in-widget-tree`) |
| Async lifecycle guards need an epoch counter. | high | correctness | prose: <100 words |
| Real I/O in testWidgets needs runAsync | high | correctness | prose: <100 words |
| Verify plugin APIs against installed source | high | correctness | prose: <50 words |
| flutter analyze at zero issues | medium | complexity | prose: <50 words |
| Sandboxed/CI runners | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words |

## Checks

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `flutter/network-fetch-in-widget-tree` | medium | complexity | check: blocking |
| `flutter/device-clock-not-injected` | high | correctness | check: blocking |

`flutter/device-clock-not-injected` stands where a prose rule used to: the clock is already named
as a port by the architecture rule above it, so the check and its fix line carry the rest.

The golden mechanics are the [`flutter-golden-tests`](skills/flutter-golden-tests/SKILL.md) skill
and lockfile skew is [`flutter-pubspec`](skills/flutter-pubspec/SKILL.md); each forces itself for
the files it concerns.

## Skills

| Skill | Trigger |
|---|---|
| [`flutter-golden-tests`](skills/flutter-golden-tests/SKILL.md) | any edit of a `*_test.dart` or a Dart file under `test/` — held by the guard until loaded |
| [`flutter-pubspec`](skills/flutter-pubspec/SKILL.md) | any edit of `pubspec.yaml` or `pubspec.lock` — held by the guard until loaded |

## Environment

The Claude Code web sandbox boots without a Flutter SDK, so `flutter test`, `flutter analyze` and
golden regeneration can't run until it is installed. The install belongs in the environment
**image** (built once, snapshotted, reused), never a per-session hook that reinstalls every start:
this pack declares that need in its `env` block ([pack.mjs](pack.mjs)), and a project pastes one
generic `environment-setup-command.sh` that runs every active pack's requirement via
[engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs](../../engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs) and asserts
it at session start (see [bootstrap.md](../../bootstrap.md) Part 9).
=== PACK.MJS ===
// Prose, two checks and one environment requirement. Both checks are forbidden
// patterns over the shipped Dart tree — a fetch the widget tree performs itself,
// and a time read off the device clock — declared beside this manifest because
// their whole logic is patterns over files. Everything else here stays prose: the
// import boundary needs a project-supplied list of forbidden plugin prefixes, and
// the rest is golden and toolchain judgment no scan can separate from healthy
// code. Fingerprint: a pubspec.yaml at the repo
// root OR one directory down (a monorepo's app/ or client/ dir) — but never
// deeper, so a stray pubspec.yaml in a nested example/fixture tree can't trip
// detection.
const hasMarkerNearRoot = (ctx, marker) =>
  ctx.tracked.some((f) => {
    const parts = f.split('/');
    return parts[parts.length - 1] === marker && parts.length <= 2;
  });

export default {
  version: '60920.2',
  minEngineVersion: '60822.1',
  ruleRoutingGuidance: {
    belongs: 'widget-tree architecture, ports and fakes, widget-test and golden mechanics, pub and analyze toolchain habits for Flutter',
    excludes: 'native Android or iOS module concerns — android and ios; store shipping — play-store-release, app-store-release',
  },
  marker: 'pubspec.yaml (at the repo root or one directory down)',
  detect: (ctx) => hasMarkerNearRoot(ctx, 'pubspec.yaml'),
  // The Flutter SDK isn't in the Claude Code Web base image, so a cloud session
  // can't run `flutter test` / analyze / golden regen without it. This declares
  // how the environment installs it (aggregated into environment-setup-command.sh) and
  // how the SessionStart check asserts it — see engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs.
  env: {
    label: 'Flutter SDK',
    setup: [
      'if [ ! -x /opt/flutter/bin/flutter ]; then',
      '  git clone --depth 1 -b stable https://github.com/flutter/flutter.git /opt/flutter',
      'fi',
      'ln -sf /opt/flutter/bin/flutter /usr/local/bin/flutter',
      'ln -sf /opt/flutter/bin/dart /usr/local/bin/dart',
      'git config --global --add safe.directory /opt/flutter || true',
      'flutter --version || true',
      'flutter precache || true   # warm host engine artifacts so the first test is fast',
    ].join('\n'),
    probe: 'command -v flutter >/dev/null 2>&1',
  },
};

The RULES.md sweeps' shape, applied to the skills against `writing-pack-prose`'s test: a `SKILL.md` may carry procedure at length, but every line must still change what the reader does. Twenty-two openings didn't.

A mounted skill means a declared pack, so those rules are loaded; the sentence sends nobody anywhere. Pointers to *other on-demand* skills stay (`repo-text-sweeps` → `git-github-advanced` for merge-time relocations, `authoring-agent-docs` → `writing-pack-prose`), because those change which doc gets opened next.

 # AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model)
 
-Portable, project-agnostic gotchas for the AWS Serverless Application Model and the API-Gateway/CloudFront stack it deploys — true for any SAM project read cold.
-
 - **esbuild must be a regular `dependency`, not a `devDependency`.** SAM's esbuild builder runs a *production-only* `npm install` in its scratch dir, so a `devDependency` esbuild is skipped and the build fails with "Cannot find esbuild." Declare it in `dependencies`, or put it on the runner's `PATH` before `sam build`. (1)
 - **CloudFront won't forward `Authorization` via a *custom* origin-request policy** — a custom `AWS::CloudFront::OriginRequestPolicy` listing `Authorization` is rejected at deploy ("The parameter Headers contains Authorization that is not allowed"). To forward it to the origin while keeping it out of the cache key (so public GETs share one cached entry), attach the **managed** `AllViewerExceptHostHeader` policy (id `b689b0a8-53d0-40ab-baf2-68738e2966ac`) plus a custom cache policy that omits `Authorization`. Use the *ExceptHostHeader* variant specifically: forwarding the viewer `Host` to an API Gateway origin returns 403. (2)
 - **A deploy role must be able to drive the transform and CloudFront, or change-set creation fails with the real reason hidden.** The `Serverless-2016-10-31` transform runs as a macro, so the deploy principal needs `cloudformation:*`, and CloudFront management needs `cloudfront:*`, both at `Resource: "*"` (scope the *data-plane* grants to your stack instead). `sam deploy` surfaces only `Waiter ChangeSetCreateComplete failed` — the actual `AccessDenied` is visible only in the CloudFormation console's **Change sets** tab. Don't paper over it with `AdministratorAccess`.

Action to specify what pull request data needs to be retrieved from GitHub. 
Possible options: 
 1. get - Get details of a specific pull request.
 2. get_diff - Get the diff of a pull request.
 3. get_status - Get combined commit status of a head commit in a pull request.
 4. get_files - Get the list of files changed in a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.

    Pattern-check engine: structured-data (parsed JSON/YAML) assertions (#820)
    
    The Category-3 append: checks whose subject is a parsed document's fields
    become declarations. Documents are parsed at most once per scan (.json via
    JSON.parse, .ya?ml via the minimal YAML parser), shared by every rule; an
    absent or unparsable document asserts nothing. Field paths are dotted;
    presence = value !== undefined.
    
    New spec vocabulary:
    - checkParsedFile: where whenFieldPresent holds, requireField must be
      present / forbidField must not;
    - equalParsedValues: two parsed fields must be equal — the first file
      selected by a path+content probe, an absent second file and a mismatch
      each firing their own declared message ({first}/{second} interpolate);
    - forEachParsedEntry: iterate a document's named entries (e.g. SAM
      Resources) filtered by field equality, forbidding an array value
      ({entry} interpolates the entry name);
    - checkKeyValueFile: dotenv-style schema — file exists, KEY=value lines
      only, closed key set, every key declared ({key}/{keys}/{line});
    - two new relevance gates: someTrackedFileContains { pathMatching, text }
      and exactlyOneTrackedFileMatches.
    
    Converted, messages and behavior preserved (all existing pack tests pass
    unchanged): cer/version-sync, cer/release-config,
    aws-sam/cloudfront-authorization, aws-sam/esbuild-dependency.
    
    Kept as code deliberately: the firebase functions pair (two-document join
    via the shared functionsCodebases lib), aws-sam/handler-path (derived
    comparison), growth-config (in-memory config, per-field prose),
    cer/privacy-permission-alignment (shares requestedPermissions with its
    work-scoped sibling — one extraction, one home), and
    web-speech-no-window-api-in-service-worker (needs a parsed-field→file-set
    feed).

{"number":242,"title":"Stage 1 spec: code planner for the fleet daily maintenance routine","body":"Spec-only PR (no implementation code yet) — the reviewable Stage 1 design before we build. Closes the design half of #241.

## What this adds

`routines/fleet/DESIGN.md` — the agreed design for turning the daily maintenance routine from "fan an agent out to every task × every repo, decide in-session" into **code decides, agents act**:

- **Task registry of `(gate, worker)` pairs.** `gate` = "should I run" (code, in the planner); `worker` = "what to do" (a doc a subagent runs, fed the gate's `targets`). Pack tasks register via a new **`maintenance: [...]`** field on `pack.mjs`, exactly like `rules`/`skills`/`env` — so a task is `scope: "fleet"` or `scope: "pack:<name>"` and the engine discovers it with no orchestrator edit.
- **The planner runs in code**, in the existing fleet-coverage Action (fleet PAT). The **entire worklist is computed before any worker agent spawns** — a task with nothing to do costs an API read, not a model turn.
- **Orchestrator = the routine session itself** (trigger + dispatch in one run). The planner is the only out-of-process piece; worker subagents are its children.
- **Stateless daily loop** (~25h UTC window) + **weekly full sweep** staggered by `hash(full_name) % 7 == UTC weekday` — ~1/7 of the fleet full-sweeps each night, and that weekly pass is the self-healing safety net (no persisted watermark).
- **Correctness invariants** baked in: landed/implemented tests key off a `mainMoved` signal (not per-object recency), and `canonChanged` excludes the plan/tracker/orchestration artifacts so the engine can't self-trigger dedup.
- **One fleet walk, three outputs** — coverage census + migration-retirement (both existing) + the new work plan. Stage 1 extends `check-fleet-coverage.mjs` in place (it's central-only; a rename would force a canon-wide reference sweep) and factors gates/signals into `routines/fleet/` modules.
- **Proves the pack seam** with `chrome-store-release` as the first real pack task.

## Blast radius

Small: the planner and every gate run **centrally** in the home repo's Action. No consumer executes new code; a member contributes only its existing `.claudinite-checks.json` (read, never written).

## Not in this PR

Implementation (`signals.mjs`, `gates.mjs`, `tasks/`, the pack task, the orchestrator rewrite) — that follows once the spec is approved. Stage 2 (narrow per-object worker skills) is deferred.

## Coordination note

There are related in-flight branches (`claude/chrome-store-release-schedule-*`, `claude/open-branches-status-*`) that overlap this area by name. Neither is merged, and neither appears to have created a fleet-maintenance seam, but worth a glance before implementation to avoid duplicated effort.

Refs #241

{"number":958,"title":"Promote fleet-digest into the sheepdog pack","body":"The fleet's daily operations brief lived as a local pack in the enforcer repo (`missingbulb/Sheepdog`, `.claudinite/local/packs/sheepdog-local/`). Shepherd is replacing Sheepdog as the enforcer, so the alternative to promoting it was a second repo's local copy of the same mechanic — the tell that it belongs centrally.

## Why it turned out to be portable

The local pack's own reasoning for staying local was that a brief is addressed to *this* fleet's owner, at an address only that repo knows, about what *this* owner counts as an accomplishment. Neither half survived contact with the code:

- **No address.** The task ends at a written file. An ad-hoc session reads the dated brief out later in the day and its own notification mechanism carries it — so there is no recipient, no sender and no transport anywhere in the task.
- **No fleet-specific taste.** What a fleet has an opinion about is `pick` (how many items the brief names) and `nudge` (the quiet-project prod). Two knobs, both defaulted.

What is left is the fleet-shaped half — enumerate the members, rank a day by size, filter the machine's own artifacts out — which is this pack's whole subject. The code needed no changes beyond import paths.

## What lands

**`packs/sheepdog/tasks/fleet-digest/`** — a sixth task, `daily+1h`.

- `worker.mjs` — prework. Collects each requested day and sorts it into three piles: already written, quiet, needing judgment. Quiet days land as one PR with no agent; the rest push a shortlist to a force-pushed data branch and request the agent. Backfill rides the scheduler's existing override bag (`FORCE_TASKS=fleet-digest,DIGEST_BACKFILL_DAYS=7`), bounded at 30 days, skipping days that already have a brief.
- `collect-fleet-day.mjs` — one UTC day, ranked. Size is arithmetic, importance is judgment: this ranks by lines touched (issues converted to line-equivalents), and `task.md` owns the picking. `isMaintenance`/`isMachineIssue` filter Claudinite's own PRs and dispatch issues out of **both** streams.
- `task.md` — the agent stage. Read the shortlist, pick `pick` of them, write the dated brief, land one PR for the run.
- `digest-config.mjs` — the `digest` config block reader. In the task folder rather than beside `fleet-config.mjs` because nothing else reads it.

**Two checks**, same folder for the same reason, wired into `pack.mjs` `worldRules`:

- `digest-plain-text` (blocking) — a brief is plain text despite its `.md` name. It is *sent*, verbatim, through a renderer that neither parses markdown nor keeps line breaks.
- `dated-fixture-collision` (blocking) — no test fixture builds a `digests/` path in the 20xx range. A fixture sharing that namespace with real briefs breaks when one is deleted and passes for the wrong reason when one happens to exist.

**Config** — an optional `digest` block on the `sheepdog` entry. Every key defaults, so an existing enforcer config keeps working untouched.

**Version** — `sheepdog` 1 → 2, to deliver the new files to enforcers already on v1. Purely additive: nothing in a member is rewritten, so no migration record.

**Secrets** — no new one. `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` gains only **Pull requests: read** over what the census already asks for.

## `packs/sheepdog/RULES.md`, rewritten as instructions (3rd commit)

The file was 242 lines describing the pack — what each sweep does, why it exists, what its report contains, what each config key means. A session loads it every time and could not act on most of it.

It is now **13 rules and 96 lines**, each keyed to the act that brings a reader to it: configuring the fleet, acting on what a sweep reports, running the manual levers, holding the PAT. The two levers ship their literal `overrides:` line in a fenced block rather than naming a script, which is what the corpus measured as the difference between 0-in-5 and 5-in-5 first-try invocations.

The description moves to `README.md`, which already carried most of it and now also holds the config schema and per-key table, how the tasks are wired (frequency, model, outcome, and the cadence reasoning), the pack-seed sweep's three safety properties, the trust model, undecidable-is-not-a-non-match, and the failure semantics. `README.md` gains the rule index the corpus expects of a pack whose prose is enumerable.

**One rule leaves this pack entirely.** "Filter the machine's own artifacts out of every stream" governs code in the sheepdog tasks — and no session that loads this file can edit that code, because the mount is read-only in a member. Canon, where the sweeps are actually written, does not declare the `sheepdog` pack at all, so no canon session ever loads it either. It moves to the enforcer's own local pack (missingbulb/Shepherd#29).

That routing problem is worth flagging beyond this PR: it is true of every "how to write a sweep" rule the file used to carry, which is most of why the rewrite is a subtraction.

## Two things I changed rather than copied

Both were tests that asserted against the enforcer repo's own state, which canon does not have — and which the enforcer's own `RULES.md` already names as an anti-pattern ("a local test that reads a canon path is coupled to canon's deletions"):

1. `dated-fixture-collision`'s last case read the enforcer's `worker.test.mjs` by its old path. Repointed at the digest's own test file, which is what the rule is actually there to keep honest.
2. `digest-plain-text`'s last case walked the enforcer's real `digests/` directory and asserted the whole series was clean. Canon carries no series, and a case that read one from here would be either permanently skipped or asserting against state that lives somewhere else. Replaced with the same assertion over a brief in exactly the format the worker and `task.md` emit; the landed series stays guarded by this same rule running as a world check in the repo that writes it.

## Verification

- **56 ported tests green**, and mutation-checked rather than assumed: `DEFAULT_PICK` 4→5, the backtick rule disabled, the collision regex flipped 20xx→19xx, `MAX_BACKFILL` 30→300, and the maintenance title test removed each turn the suite red (1, 2, 4, 1 and 2 failures); restoring goes back to 56/56.
- **Full canon suite green** — 1908 tests across `packs-tests/` and `engine-tests/`.
- **`check_the_world`: 0 blocking, 60 advisory** — one *below* `main`'s 61, because `packs/sheepdog/RULES.md` no longer raises `rules-line-length` at all (it was 75 over-length lines).

## Merged `main` (4th commit)

#957 landed the Sheepdog → Shepherd reference sweep while this was open. It touched none of the files this branch rewrites, so the only conflict was the corpus tally in `packs/README.md` — derived data, so the markers were cleared and the figure re-derived from the merged tree rather than hand-merged.

CI did not fire on the last two pushes (GitHub's recursion guard suppresses `pull_request` runs for pushes authored by a token-backed identity), so the suite was started with the `workflow_dispatch` `ci.yml` carries for exactly that case.

## Follow-ups, not in this PR

- `missingbulb/Sheepdog` holds the only other copy. It should not be archived or deleted until this lands.
- Shepherd's `digests/README.md` (carried over in missingbulb/Shepherd#23) says the task lives "in this repo's own local pack" — true of Sheepdog, and stale once this lands. Its own change.
- The enforcer's `sheepdog-local/RULES.md` carries ~360 lines of lessons, about half of them generic harness/Claudinite ones that would serve every member. Flagged at the bottom of #954.

{"number":1028,"title":"sheepdog: judge fleet freshness by stamped versions, not ref age","body":"Fixes #1025.

## The bug

`fleet-roster`'s `behind` state measured the **age of the stamped ref**. The versioned update flows deliberately never rewrite `ref`, so every member's stamp is frozen at whatever commit first vendored it — and every member's ref ages at the same rate. With the fleet stamped at `631a067` (2026-08-13) and `staleDays: 14`, the condition would have gone true for **every member at once on 2026-08-27**, opening a `fleet-drift` issue per repo for a fleet that is, by versions, current.

## What `behind` measures now

The **version gap**, and nothing else:

- stamped `engineVersion` below canon's `ENGINE_VERSION`, or
- any stamped `packVersions` entry below that pack's manifest `version` in canon,

with the gap named in the drift issue (`behind canon by engine v3 → v4, basics v5 → v7`).

Both numbers are read out of **canon** over the API — `engine/version.mjs` and each pack's `pack.mjs` — never out of the enforcer's own mount, which is itself a member and can be behind. The reader is memoized per sweep, so canon is read once per *distinct pack* across the whole walk rather than once per member.

Two shapes the classifier refuses to guess at: a pack canon has retired has no manifest to be behind and contributes no gap (an absent number never reads as zero), and a manifest that is present but whose version can't be parsed **throws**, which becomes `unknown` for that member and fails the run.

A stamp carrying neither number is `behind` by construction — an engine that stamps always stamps.

## What is unchanged

`no-stamp`, `no-scheduler` and `ref-not-on-trunk` all read the ref for what it still honestly is, provenance. The compare call stays for the `ref-not-on-trunk` wedge (#328); only its `ahead_by` and base-commit date are no longer read.

The body marker still spells `fleet-freshness` and the `behind` state token is unchanged, so open drift issues are read rather than re-opened as `unrecorded`.

## `staleDays`

With no date measure left it governs nothing, so it is retired from `parseSheepdogConfig`, from the report header, from the drift issue body and from the docs. An enforcer config still carrying the key is read, not rejected — unknown keys were always ignored.

## Also

- `packs/sheepdog/pack.mjs` version 7 → 8 (delivery signal).
- `task.md`'s "the one assumption" section rewritten; its pointer to the closed #786 removed.
- `RULES.md`'s "judging whether a member is behind" bullet no longer claims `staleDays` governs a legacy measure.

## Verification

- New tests written first and watched fail (the module had no `canonVersions` export), then green.
- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` on the rebased head: 2131 pass, 1 fail — `engine-pack-lane-shims`, which fails identically on a stashed tree ("this checkout is too shallow to walk origin/main's pack history").
- `check_the_work`: clean. `check_the_world`: 0 blocking, and the one advisory this change introduced (`task-phase-discipline`) was removed by rewording rather than waived.
- Rebased onto `cae5273` after #1013 landed; its `prework` → `code_work` rename conflicted with the `staleDays` removal on one README line, both sides kept.

{"number":1052,"title":"sheepdog: state the FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN grant in one place","body":"Fixes #1030.

The permission list was spelled in seven places, each the subset its own author needed. Those strings were the only machine-readable statement of the requirement, so a human assembling a grant out of them landed the union of the subsets and missed `Pull requests: read` — needed only by the digest, and only once a member is private.

## What changed

**`packs/sheepdog/`** — new `fleet-token.mjs`: one table, a row per fine-grained-PAT permission carrying the access to grant, why it is needed, which sweep uses it at what level, and the endpoints it covers. Everything about the token now renders from it:

- every sweep's "token is not set" message names the **whole** grant first, then that sweep's own subset as explanation (`missingFleetTokenError`). The six hand-written strings are gone.
- `pack.mjs` gains `adoptionHandover` built from the table, so the adopting session files a checkbox carrying the complete list — ask 2. It also bumps `version` to 10 so enforcers already on 9 receive this.
- `fleet-api.mjs` attributes a `403` to the permission that would fix it, on `paged`, `readFile`, `fileExists`, `putFile` and `classifyDispatch`. This is the cheaper half of the preflight in ask 3: no extra requests, and it reports on the call that actually failed rather than on a probe that may not resemble it. A path no row claims gets no hint — a wrong guess is worse than none.
- `RULES.md`, `README.md`, the task `task.md`/`task.mjs` comments: the lists are replaced by a pointer at the table. Narrative mentions of a single permission ("dispatching is an Actions write") stay.

**`packs-tests/sheepdog/`** — `fleet-token.test.mjs` drives each of the six sweeps' real `main()` with the secret unset and asserts every permission in the table appears; asserts adoption hands over the complete grant; asserts the `403` attribution; and scans every tracked file in the pack for a permission **list** (two or more name+access pairs within two lines) outside `fleet-token.mjs`. Run against the pre-change content that last test flags all seven sites and nothing after. Two older tests asserted the wording that is now retired and were updated.

## Not done

A preflight probe per permission. It cannot be accurate where it matters: `Pull requests: read` fails only on a **private** member, so a probe against the enforcer's own repo would pass on a grant that later 403s, and a probe against a private member is the same request the sweep is about to make anyway. The 403 attribution gets the diagnosis without the guess. Happy to add one if you want it regardless.

method.description:
Action to specify what pull request data needs to be retrieved from GitHub. 
Possible options: 
 1. get - Get details of a specific pull request.
 2. get_diff - Get the diff of a pull request.
 3. get_status - Get combined commit status of a head commit in a pull request.
 4. get_files - Get the list of files changed in a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 5. get_commits - Get the list of commits on a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 6. get_review_comments - Get review threads on a pull request. Each thread contains logically grouped review comments made on the same code location during pull request reviews. Returns thread metadata and comments with nullable current and original line-range coordinates (line, start_line, original_line, original_start_line). Current coordinates are omitted when unavailable, such as for outdated comments. Use cursor-based pagination (perPage, after) to control results.
 7. get_reviews - Get the reviews on a pull request. When asked for review comments, use get_review_comments method. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 8. get_comments - Get comments on a pull request. Use this if user doesn't specifically want review comments. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 9. get_check_runs - Get check runs for the head commit of a pull request. Check runs are the individual CI/CD jobs and checks that run on the PR.

{"number":1081,"title":"Pack reorganization: two collapses and two renames","body":"Closes #1079.

Four pack-tree changes, plus the one engine mechanism a rename turned out to be missing.

**`github-actions` → `git-github`.** The pack held the workflow-YAML rules and the scheduling skill, kept apart from the git/GitHub procedure they are the platform half of by a fingerprint that was redundant: every `gha/` check already selects its inputs from `.github/workflows/`, so a repo with no workflows heard from none of them, and a repo with workflows had to declare a second pack to be told so. Nine checks (not one — the issue said so), the skill and the routing move; the `gha/` ids stay, because a member's `accept` entries name rules by id. `static-website` stops naming it in `requires` — git-github arrives through `basics` on its own.

**`firebase-release` → `firebase`, as the `create-release-plan` skill.** The release standard was a second declaration a project added once it decided it was ready to ship — content read at one moment in a project's life, which is what a skill is for.

**`canary-probe` → `claudinite-canary-repo`** and **`sheepdog` → `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog`** — the prefix a pack carries when its subject is a Claudinite feature.

**The engine half.** All four go through `RENAMED_PACKS` plus a declaration-converging record, as the last two renames did. What was missing is the other side of a rename: vendoring replaces a tree per declared id, so the directory a pack used to be vendored under matched nothing afterwards and stayed in the mount forever — announcing, once the loader canonicalized it, the *same id* as the live one. The pack flow now sweeps it as a property of renaming, so no future rename has to remember to.

The enforcer's config is the part a rename can genuinely break, because it is a fact the enforcer wrote and a declaration converges on its own schedule: the fleet-config reader, the dashboard's legacy-source lookup and the two dormant fleet-baseline records all match the entry through the rename map, and the legacy `packConfig` key is still read under the spelling it was written with.

## Folders touched

- **`packs/git-github/`** — gains `declared-checks.json`, the `github-actions-scheduling` skill, the collapse record; manifest and README rewritten around them.
- **`packs/firebase/`** — gains `skills/create-release-plan/` and the collapse record.
- **`packs/claudinite-canary-repo/`, `packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/`** — renamed from `canary-probe` / `sheepdog`, each with its rename record; the sheepdog config reader now resolves either spelling.
- **`packs/claudinite-dashboard/`** — its legacy enforcer-entry lookup resolves either spelling.
- **`engine/pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs`** — four new entries. **`engine/scheduler/`** — three comments stop naming the pack (the new id is hyphenated, so the barrier sees them).
- **`updates/pack-update.mjs`** — the abandoned-mount-directory sweep.
- **`dev/tools/badges/render.mjs`** — `restyle` takes a badge's id from its path, so a rename no longer leaves the old name in the title and gradient id with the tool reporting nothing to do.
- **`packs/{basics,chrome-extension,claudinite-*,headless-browser,macos,static-website,web-scraping,app-store-release,play-store-release,android,ios,tidy-repo}/`** — routing guidance repointed at the surviving pack, version bumped.
- **`.claudinite-checks.json`** — this repo drops its `github-actions` declaration; barrier exceptions follow the renames.

## Verification

`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` → 2249 pass, 1 fail: `every engine module a fielded pack version imports still resolves`, which aborts on `this checkout is too shallow to walk origin/main's pack history`. It fails identically on unmodified `main` in this sandbox and needs a depth-0 fetch, which CI does.

`check_the_work` and `check_the_world` are both clean (0 blocking).

{"number":1222,"title":"One shared git-tree delete, and a beat that does not read the clock","body":"Both tests in #1219 reddened CI on #1218, whose diff touched neither.

### The rimraf race — fixed at the cause, not at the call site

`ENOTEMPTY` on a temp `.git` has now been closed three times (#235, #258, #1219) and come back twice. The reason is visible in the pattern: each fix repaired the one call site that happened to fail, while every other site kept spelling its own bare `rmSync`. So this moves the retry into **`engine/remove-tree.mjs`**, once, with the whole story of why; the 127 sites that delete a tree call it; and a guard test fails when a new site spells the delete by hand.

The guard is the part that matters — and it earned its keep immediately: my own "files that drive git" heuristic found 13 files, and the guard then found **9 more sites in 2 files** it had missed. `engine-tests/helpers.mjs`'s existing `cleanup()` now delegates to the same helper, so there is one implementation rather than two.

One correction to the issue's framing, from reading the code around the fix: the retry is the **second** line of defense, not the first. #235's real fix was `GIT_ENV` keeping git's auto-gc and maintenance in the foreground so no detached process outlives a fixture command. Both comments now say which is which, so the next reader doesn't mistake the retry for the cure.

### The heartbeat beat — no clock at all

The three beat tests started a 5 ms interval and waited 40 ms of real time for at least 2 beats — 2 of a possible 8, which a loaded runner coalescing timers fails. All three now drive `t.mock.timers`, so the assertion is exact (N intervals ticked ⇒ N beats) instead of probabilistic, and the file runs in 121 ms instead of sleeping through 100 ms of it. A comment says not to reintroduce a real `setTimeout` wait "to give the beat a chance", since that is the bug.

### Proving it

- Reverting `clearInterval` reds 2 of the rewritten beat tests; making the beat never fire reds 2 others.
- Re-introducing one bare `rmSync(..., { recursive: true })` reds the guard, naming the file and line.
- Emptying the guard's own scope reds its companion test — a sweep guard that matches nothing reads green forever otherwise.

The suite caught one real consequence I'd have missed: `vendoring/apply-vendor-set.mjs` is copied into a hand-curated scratch canon by its fixture, so its new import needed a copy line in both fixture builders. That is the fixture doing its job.

Full suite 2543 green; `check_the_work` 0 blocking (after the two pack version bumps and their `VERSIONS.md` rows); `check_the_world` 0 blocking; the consumer rehearsal 40 green across all shapes and both modes.

One advisory left deliberately: `file-placement` flags `vendoring/rehearsal/rehearse.mjs` reaching `engine/remove-tree.mjs` at distance 3. Its own remedy text exempts "a deliberate cross-cutting concern", which a single shared delete is.

Closes #1219

{"number":1294,"title":"fleet-baseline: follow every member to current, report outcomes not dispatches","body":"Closes #1293

## The problem

A dispatch POST returning 204 says a run was **queued** and nothing more. A report built from those 204s describes the sweep's own outgoing calls while reading as fleet-wide delivery. #1292 recorded the cost: a run announced `13 fired, 0 failed` while 9 of the 13 took nothing.

## What it does now

After firing, the sweep follows each dispatched member until a terminal condition read **off the member itself** — does its own `.claudinite-settings.json` stamp the engine and every declared pack at the versions canon publishes?

| Outcome | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `converged` | was behind canon, reached its versions during this run |
| `already-current` | was at canon's versions before the dispatch, so its update correctly declined |
| `did-not-converge` | its scheduler ran and it is still behind — go and read it |
| `never-started` | the dispatch was accepted and no run followed it |
| `unknown` | the member could not be read |

The headline becomes **`current of dispatched`**, and the run **fails** when a dispatched member never got there — the case the old report counted as a win.

`already-current` is a success in its own right, and a distinct one. Such a member's `update` precondition correctly declines and it does no work; folding it into a failure would report a fault where there is none, and into `converged` would claim work that did not happen. Reading it requires a freshness probe *before* the dispatch, which is where that read now happens.

## Reuse, not reimplementation

`canonVersions` and `classifyFreshness` already existed in this pack for the roster's drift issues. They are imported, not copied — same pack, so no cross-pack dependency.

## This is not #649's sleep coming back

That follow was a **blind fixed wait** every run paid whatever the fleet was doing, and it forced the lever to be a standalone workflow with a `.github/` managed copy. `follow-to-current.mjs` polls a **real terminal condition** and each member leaves the loop the moment it reads current — an already-current fleet finishes on the first pass in seconds, and the lever stays an ordinary queue task.

`code_work_timeout` rises 900s → 1800s so the 20-minute follow budget (`FOLLOW_MINUTES`, overridable per item) finishes well inside it. A run the platform kills never prints the report it spent the time earning, and there's a test asserting that margin holds.

## The limitation, stated in the report itself

"Current" is a claim about **published version numbers**. Canon content shipped without a version bump moves no number, so a member can read `already-current` while lacking canon's newest commit — exactly the #1292 case. The report says this in its own words rather than letting the word imply more than was checked.

## Purging the reversed decision

The old "it does not wait" is written down in several places, and all of them are now wrong. Removed from the pack `RULES.md`, both `README.md`s, and the task test literally named *"…and never follows"* — replaced there by a test of the bound that makes the follow safe.

## Verification

- Full suite: **2708 pass, 0 fail**. `check_the_world`: 0 blocking. `check_the_work`: clean.
- 19 new tests, clock and sleep injected so nothing waits.
- See-it-fail on every new assertion: collapsing `already-current` into `converged`, treating a timed-out member as success, dropping the never-started distinction, reverting the headline to a dispatch count, removing the follow-failure escalation, and dropping the limitation note — each went red, then green.

**Not yet exercised against the real fleet.** I can drive it once merged, which is also the honest test of whether the 20-minute budget matches what members actually take.

{"number":755,"title":"Promote two store/seed checks from Sheepdog PR #110 to the canon","body":"Sheepdog [#110](https://github.com/missingbulb/Sheepdog/pull/110) proposed a local `preferences-store` pack and was closed. Its [closing comment](https://github.com/missingbulb/Sheepdog/pull/110#issuecomment-5255280747) records that two of its checks are worth keeping but belong in the canon rather than in a member. This lands both, from that PR's diff.

## (a) `preferences-store-file-names` → `packs/claude-code-web-users-support/`

Every file in a preferences store is `README.md` or `<identity>.md`. That is a property of **being a store**, not of Sheepdog — the same feature the canon pack already owns.

- It sits beside `store.mjs` and imports `resolveStore` / `isUsableIdentity` as **siblings**, so it can never be stricter or looser than the code that opens a person's file. #110 had to reach across the vendored mount to get the same guarantee, which is exactly what forced it to carry a `file-placement` acceptance in `.claudinite-checks.json`; here there is nothing to excuse.
- **Advisory**, matching its sibling `store-configured` for the same reason: the loss is a nicety no other check or task depends on, and the fix is a rename.
- **Relevance-gated** on the repo actually holding the store directory its own declaration names, so it is inert in every member that merely declares the pack to *read* a store living elsewhere.
- It reads the store off `ctx.config.packConfig` — the engine's normalized per-pack view, the way `store-configured` does — rather than re-parsing `.claudinite-checks.json` as the local-pack version did.

## (b) `fleet-pack-seed-agrees` → `packs/sheepdog/`

The pack-agnostic form of #110's `store-address-agrees`. That version compared a `packSeeds` entry against the repo's own declaration of the pack, but hardcoded `claude-code-web-users-support` and `resolveStore`. Generalized: **for any seeded pack the enforcer also declares itself, the seed's config and the local config must agree.**

- Naming no pack preserves the sheepdog pack's deliberate design — the same "the enforcer names no pack" rule `fleet-config.mjs` and the seed sweep already hold to. The seeded ids are the whole vocabulary.
- Because it may not know any pack's defaults, agreement is **exact value equality** (key-order-insensitive). The cost is spelling a default out on both sides; the benefit is a comparison that cannot be wrong about a pack it has never heard of.
- **Blocking.** The seed sweep writes into every member and never overrides, so a wrong seed reaches the fleet once and then sticks — correcting it in the enforcer un-writes nothing.
- Seeds are read through `fleet-config.mjs`'s one parser, so the seeds judged are exactly the seeds that would be written (it drops the malformed ones); the local side is read through the engine's normalized config, the way a session in this repo actually runs the pack. A pack the fleet standardizes on but the enforcer does not itself declare is out of scope.

## consumer-safe-change: fixture, not a migration record

`fleet-pack-seed-agrees` is a new blocking rule, so `consumer-safe-change` asks for one of the two. **The fixture is the honest answer here** — the change is additive: nothing is renamed, and nothing new is required of a member that was already conforming. There is no fleet to move across, only a shape to prove stays green.

The new `sheepdog-enforcer` rehearsal shape is a repo declaring `sheepdog` with a `packSeeds` entry *and* its own declaration of the seeded pack — the two configs the rule now compares. They agree, so the enforcer converges green in both rehearsal modes. Confirmed the fixture actually exercises the rule rather than passing vacuously: making the two disagree turns the rehearsal red naming `fleet-pack-seed-agrees`, and it was then restored.

Checked the real fleet too — the one enforcer that exists today already states `{ "repo": "missingbulb/Sheepdog" }` on both sides, so nothing goes red overnight.

## Tests

Both see-it-fail fixtures come across, into `packs-tests/`, each asserting the claimed defect against the real reader (`store.mjs`'s `fileFor`; `parseSheepdogConfig`) rather than restating it. The seed fixture uses a made-up pack id throughout — a test reaching for a real one would quietly become a test of that pack.

Verified: full suite green (1415 tests before the rehearsal shape, 16/16 on the rehearsal gate after); `check_the_world.mjs` at 0 blocking with no new advisories; `check_the_work.mjs` clean. Each check was mutated to confirm its fixtures bite (accepting any `.md` name → 5 failures; comparing config presence instead of value → failures) before being restored.

Catalog tally moves 80 → 82, with the two per-pack counts in `packs/README.md`.

Prose: each check's `doc` pointer got the invariant it points at — the store-side naming rule in the web-users pack, the two-places-must-agree rule in sheepdog's — stated without narrating the enforcement (`pack-no-enforcement-narration` caught a first draft that named the rule id). The genuinely Sheepdog-local prose from #110 ("a preference is live here before it is live for the fleet", "correcting the seeded address does not un-seed the old one") stays in that repo, per the closing comment.","state":"closed","draft":false,"merged":true,"mergeable_state":"unknown","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/755","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"merged_by":"missingbulb","head":{"ref":"claude/sheepdog-store-seed-checks-iz9r31","sha":"5e4cecabc169ef8b679fc18c0aed3efb3f01a1ab","repo":{"full_name":"missingbulb/Claudinite"}},"base":{"ref":"main","sha":"069bf33eaa5e6dab53a6c10ff7254327df10960a","repo":{"full_name":"missingbulb/Claudinite"}},"additions":369,"deletions":5,"changed_files":10,"commits":2,"created_at":"2026-08-11T15:56:54Z","updated_at":"2026-08-11T17:30:20Z","closed_at":"2026-08-11T17:30:18Z","merged_at":"2026-08-11T17:30:18Z"}

{"number":1851,"title":"Move dormancy out of engine settings onto the scheduler's own pack","body":"Closes #1845

`dormant` was a top-level key of `.claudinite-settings.json`, validated by the engine and normalized onto the loaded config. It never belonged there: every effect it has is an effect on the work-item queue, and a repo declaring no `claudinite-tasks` has no scheduler for the word to mean anything about.

It is now a parameter of the pack that owns the mechanism:

```json
{ "id": "claudinite-tasks", "config": { "dormant": true } }
```

The predicate moved to that pack and is published through its `shared-code/` surface — the one place `pack-independence` lets another pack import across. The scheduler, the executor, the dashboard and the fleet sweeps all read that one predicate, over both shapes it must answer for: a raw declaration as a cross-repo reader fetches it, and the normalized config `loadConfig` returns.

## What the engine keeps

Two things, and nothing else:

- the retired key among its legacy keys, so a member still declaring it collects no unknown-setting error;
- a deprecated `isDormant` reading only the old spelling, because the engine and a pack reach a member on separate cycles and a fielded pack version still imports it — a missing export there is a crash mid-converge, in the flow that would have delivered the fix.

Both retire together on #1846. `loadConfig` now also returns the raw declaration, which is how a pack-owned reader reaches a key the engine deliberately no longer folds.

## Shepherd

Dormancy stops being a property of the repository. A dormant member is measured for freshness like any other and its drift reported — dormancy stops the scheduler, not the clock, and a mount several engine versions behind is behind whether or not anything there still runs. Previously the roster dropped dormant members out of the freshness half entirely, so a dormant mount could drift arbitrarily far with the sweep saying nothing at all.

The single thing the declaration now suppresses is the `no-scheduler` verdict: a member told to stop is not then reported for having stopped. Its drift issue no longer closes as *not planned*, and says instead that the gap will not close on its own, since the fan-out leaves dormant members alone.

## One decision I made against the brief

You picked the hybrid — fan-outs that already dispatch drop their pre-filter and let the member's scheduler self-skip. Implementing it turned up two reasons not to, so `fleet-baseline` keeps its filter:

1. **It was never a second authority.** It calls the member's own predicate, re-exported. There is one definition and two call sites, so there is no disagreement to remove — only a dispatch per dormant member to spend learning what the declaration in hand already said.
2. **It would silently break `INCLUDE_DORMANT`.** The member's own gate stops a woken run too, so every forced dispatch would self-skip while the sweep reported `fired` — a config channel that stops being read and defaults silently.

The gate that causes (2) is itself wrong, and is filed separately as #1849: the dormancy check runs before the forced-wake block, so `INCLUDE_DORMANT=true` is already a no-op today. Fixing it changes when a dormant repo runs something, so it wants its own review.

## Dashboard

The work block hides its tasks elements when the scheduler is dormant, with a note saying why. Every row there is otherwise a task that cannot run and an item nothing will move — drawn as usual they read as a badly stuck repo, which is the one impression the block exists to give accurately.

## Migration

A record moves the key, through a new declarative op that lifts a top-level setting onto its owning pack's entry. Structural rather than textual: the target is nested inside an entry object inside the `packs` array, which no anchored pattern reaches across. Where the pack is not declared the key is dropped rather than moved; where the entry already answers, that answer stands.

## Verification

Full suite green (3374 passing), `check_the_world` and `check_the_work` both clean. Each new assertion was seen red first, and the ones that pass by construction — the predicate's three read paths, the migration op, the dormant/awake dashboard contrast — were confirmed by mutating the code under them and watching them bite.
